newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Senate set to approve milder rebuke of Mexico.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Senate set to approve milder rebuke of Mexico.

text.p: The Senate on Thursday headed toward approval of a compromise criticising Mexico's effort in the war on drugs and setting goals for improvement, but avoiding harsher steps opposed by the White House.

The compromise, drafted by key senators in negotiations with Clinton administration officials, stops well short of overturning President Bill Clinton's February 28 finding that Mexico is cooperating fully in the anti-drug fight.

That finding, known as "certification," is required by U.S. law to spare nations like Mexico, which are sources of illegal narcotics smuggled into the United States, from facing economic sanctions for lack of cooperation. Congressional critics claim the Mexican government has been corrupted by drug money and did not deserve certification.

The Clinton administration signed off on the compromise late Wednesday when Senate negotiators dropped a provision paving the way for a congressional vote in September on whether Mexico and the United States had met the goals for improvement in Mexico's performance.

But a Senate debate and vote remained in doubt until Thursday morning because of a threat by Democrats to block all legislation in an attempt to force Republican Majority Leader Trent Lott to set a date for consideration of a separate issue, a treaty outlawing chemical weapons.
The threat was withdrawn with Lott's assurances that he would work to bring the treaty to the floor. It is bottled up in the Senate Foreign Relations Committee.

Agreement to act on the compromise Mexico bill meant that the Senate will not be faced with a divisive debate and vote on a straight resolution nullifying Clinton's ruling that Mexico was a reliable anti-drug ally.

The House of Representatives voted last week to overturn Clinton's decision but suspended the step for 90 days to give Mexico time to make specific reforms. Its action has no effect unless the Senate goes along.
Mexico reacted with fury to the House vote, and Clinton aides led by Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin began talks with key senators to head off similar action in the Senate.

The resulting Senate measure chooses its words carefully but nonetheless lists a number of specific failures in the anti-drugs effort and concludes: "There has been ineffective and insufficient progress in halting the production and transit through Mexico of illegal drugs."

It says that much of the cocaine used in the United States comes from Mexico, that there is evidence that Mexican institutions are affected by "significant corruption" and that Mexico has yet to fully implement new law against organised crime and money laundering.
It says Mexican drug cartels operate with impunity and Mexico has not honoured any U.S. requests to extradite Mexican nationals indicted in the United states on drug charges.

The measure requires a presidential report by September 1 on progress by the U.S. and Mexican governments on dismantling drug trafficking organisations, on strengthening bilateral cooperation and border enforcement and on denying safe havens to traffickers.
The report would have to detail actions on crop eradication, money laundering and criminal screening of law enforcement officers.
It calls for information on progress by the United States in anti-drug education, international drug interdiction and deployment of 1,000 additional immigration patrol agents.
